hints: Notice the given velocity starts positive, falls at a constant rate, crosses zero, then becomes increasingly negative.
Recall that the gradient of a displacement-time graph equals velocity, so the $s$-$t$ gradient must start positive, flatten to zero, then become negative.
Ask where displacement must be maximum - it is at the time when the velocity-time line crosses the $t$-axis - and which $s$-$t$ shape has a smooth zero-gradient peak there.
walkthrough: Read the velocity-time graph: it is a straight line with negative gradient, starting at positive $v$, passing through $v = 0$, then going negative. This is motion with constant negative acceleration.
Use the rule that gradient of displacement $s$ against time $t$ equals velocity $v$. So the $s$-$t$ graph must start with a positive gradient that gets less steep.
While $v$ is positive but shrinking, $s$ must still increase but with decreasing slope, giving a curve that flattens.
When $v = 0$ at the $t$-axis crossing, the $s$-$t$ gradient must be zero, so $s$ reaches a smooth maximum.
After that $v$ is negative, so the $s$-$t$ gradient must be negative and $s$ must decrease, with the curve getting steeper downward.
Only a downward-opening smooth parabola starting at the origin shows increase, zero-gradient maximum, then decrease. This is option A.

A.explanation: Smooth curve rises with decreasing gradient to a maximum then falls, matching velocity that is positive and decreasing, zero at the peak, then negative.

B.explanation: Two straight-line sections would mean two different constant velocities, not a velocity $v$ that decreases steadily through zero.

C.explanation: Displacement $s$ keeps increasing, which would need $v$ to stay positive, but the given $v$-$t$ graph crosses to negative values.

D.explanation: Sharp peak of straight lines would mean sudden reversal between constant velocities, not uniform deceleration with a smooth $s$-$t$ maximum.
